crtsh_or_bruteforce_required: Enable crt.sh, HackerTarget, DNS brute-force, a keyword search, sibling-domain brute-force, or any combination.
speed_hint_fast: High concurrency, short DNS timeout: quickest, may miss slow-to-resolve names.
speed_hint_normal: Balanced default, good for most domains.
speed_hint_cautious: Low concurrency, longer DNS timeout: gentler on the nameservers.
empty_description: Enter a domain above and click Start scan.
guide_intro: Combines five techniques real subdomain/asset enumeration tools use: two independent passive subdomain lookups, a passive broad keyword lookup, an active DNS subdomain brute-force, and an active sibling-domain brute-force.
guide_step1_body: Certificate Transparency logs record every publicly-trusted TLS certificate ever issued. Any subdomain that's ever had a certificate (via Let's Encrypt, a wildcard cert, etc.) shows up here, found without a single request to the target itself.
guide_step_hackertarget_body: Queries HackerTarget's free hostsearch API, an independent passive DNS dataset, not Certificate Transparency. It finds different names than crt.sh (and keeps working when crt.sh itself is down, which happens often since it's a free, community-run service). Worth leaving on alongside crt.sh, not instead of it.
guide_step_keyword_body: Also searches crt.sh for any certificate whose name contains a keyword anywhere, with no requirement that it share the domain's DNS hierarchy. This catches domains like <0>{{example1}}</0> that a company registered separately from <1>{{example2}}</1>: a real subdomain search can never find these, since <0>{{example1}}</0> isn't a subdomain of <1>{{example2}}</1> at all, just a similarly-named, unrelated domain. Results found this way are flagged "different domain" in the table, not implied to be part of the target's own DNS tree.
guide_step2_body: Tries common prefixes (<0>{{p1}}</0>, <1>{{p2}}</1>, <2>{{p3}}</2>, <3>{{p4}}</3>, etc.) against the domain and resolves each one. The wordlist is ranked by real-world frequency (SecLists), so "Top 100" already catches the common ones; "Top 1000+" digs deeper at the cost of more DNS traffic and time.
guide_step_sibling_body: Same wordlist as DNS brute-force, but joined with a hyphen instead of a dot: tries <0>{{example1}}</0>, <1>{{example2}}</1>, etc. as their own apex domains, not subdomains. This is the active counterpart to the keyword search above: it catches a sibling environment that resolves in DNS but was never issued a publicly-trusted certificate at all (an internal CA, a self-signed cert), so it could never show up in Certificate Transparency no matter how crt.sh is queried.
guide_step3_body: Controls the DNS brute-force step: <0>Fast</0> resolves many names at once with a short timeout; <1>Cautious</1> spaces it out with fewer parallel lookups and a longer timeout, easier on nameservers that rate-limit. <2>Normal</2> is a balanced default.
guide_step4_title: Click "Start scan" and watch it stream in
guide_step4_body: Both sources merge into one candidate list, resolved concurrently. Matches appear in the table live as DNS confirms them. "Stop" cancels a running scan at any point.
guide_step5_body: <0>Resolved</0> means the name currently has a DNS record: it's live right now. <1>Source</1> shows how it was found: <2>{{s1}}</2> or HackerTarget (certificate/DNS history), <3>{{s2}}</3> (wordlist + DNS), a keyword match, or a combination. Toggle "Show unresolved attempts" to see brute-force misses too (off by default since most of a large wordlist won't exist). A "different domain" badge means the row isn't actually a subdomain of the target, just a similarly-named domain a keyword search happened to turn up.
guide_footer_note: crt.sh lookups are passive, but DNS brute-force sends real queries toward the domain's nameservers. Only run this against domains you're authorized to test.
